# One of the Best AAA Games I’ve Ever Played

*Black Myth: Wukong* is easily one of the best AAA games I’ve played, and it has definitely earned a spot in my Top 10.

The game is heavily story-driven and draws inspiration from *Journey to the West*. I recommend learning a little about the original story beforehand if you want a deeper understanding of the game's narrative and characters. However, even if you go in completely blind, like I did, you'll still have a fantastic experience.

For me, **the combat and boss designs are among the absolute best parts of the game.** Every encounter feels exciting, and the variety of bosses keeps things interesting throughout your journey.

One thing worth mentioning is that the game isn't as punishing as many other Souls-like games. In fact, I wouldn't consider it a traditional Souls-like, despite what some people might expect. That doesn't mean it's easy, though! Certain bosses can be genuinely challenging, and you'll sometimes need to experiment with different builds, abilities, and strategies to overcome them.

The game is also packed with secrets and hidden content. There's no shame in looking things up on YouTube if you get stuck or want to discover something you missed. Even after completing the game, there's still plenty to explore, and a second playthrough can be well worth your time.

**Overall, I absolutely love this game.** It's easily one of my favourite gaming experiences and has secured a place in my personal Top 10.

I would definitely recommend *Black Myth: Wukong* if you have the patience, enjoy action RPGs, and want a game that offers fantastic combat, memorable boss fights, and a satisfying level of challenge. Absolutely worth getting!

I wanted to enjoy Black Myth: Wukong, but I could not get a clean-looking image on my 1440p RTX 5060 PC.

I tried DLSS at different resolution levels, DLAA, frame generation on and off, high texture/hair/anti-aliasing settings, ray tracing off, sharpening adjustments, and monitor settings. The main issue was that Wukong’s hair often looked dotted, grainy, or distorted. Foliage and thin environmental details also looked unstable and shimmery. Lowering sharpening made the character’s face and clothes look too blurry, while increasing it made the visual artefacts stand out even more.

The combat and world seem promising, but I spent too much time trying to fix the graphics and could not enjoy the game in this state.

Black Myth: Wukong is straight up so fun to play, 9 out of 10!! Dodge, jump and attack, are your basics here. Mix that with some pretty neat skills and abilities and you have a recipe for awesome. The basics in this game never get overly complicated, which I like. You have to dodge at the right time and strike. It's fast paced combat I really love. I got 100% achievements in Sekiro and this game reminds me of a slightly easier, but still very challenging version of that game. You're constantly fighting mini-bosses or bosses as you explore a semi open-world area, which are all very beautiful to explore. The game never lets the areas wear out it's welcome before your plunged into a new Chapter to explore. Black Myth is a fast paced, high octane, risk and reward game that is insanely addictive to play.

In my opinion the game is overhyped, bosses are pointlessly overpowered, some with 2nd stages, while you have no abilities, spells or whatsoever (especially at the start, cause fighting a single boss for 2 hours is crazy)... but for some reason I'm still playing it. It's also good for training your nerves to not break something.

Journey to the West is one of my favorite mythology tails, so I knew I'd been playing this sooner or later.
Sadly, 20ish hours in I just don't feel compelled to progress further.

There are many aspects I like: for one, haven't played a combat this satisfying since Ghost of Tsushima. Mastering your own evolving skills and learning enemies patterns really feels rewarding - choreography and cinematics are great and I never felt frustrated once.
Obscure lore is big plus for me in the way it's presented and delivered. Voices in the wind, riddles and a lot of hinting to Sun Wukong's myth are amazing. And visuals are really top notch.

But there are some huge problems that such bright sides can't hide for long.
There are basic upgrades hidden behind missable NPCs quest.
There are missable bosses and encounters that lock themselves until NG+ without any hint.
Most things don't have any trigger to signal the player something has changed, or that his actions had an impact - resulting in potentially missing stuff you actually unlocked or progressed towards.
Some bosses / encounters straight up negate some builds, not letting you use whatever playstyle suits you the most.

These points are straight up bad design choices that ultimately hinder the two best aspects of this game, leaving it carried by its visuals. If you like souls-inspired boss rushes, I'd suggest buying at a fairly discounted price.

Incredible game. Not that difficult (first tried 90% of bosses), but it doesn't have to be hard because it is so fun! I knew nothing about Journey to the West, aside from 3 things:
- Wukong is a mischievous monkey that achieved Buddhahood
- He has a boar-human friend
- He is the inspiration for Goku
So it was a bit weird seeing a bunch of talking animals, but you can still easily follow the story. So you'll still have fun. Banger music, especially "Listen Not". 

The game runs fine?????? With my laptop, the gameplay (the important part) runs smoothly on the default setting, but the cutscenes stutters a bit, which is odd since it is a cutscene? The game also has this weird afterimage effect when something moves, I don't know if it is normal, but I have seen other peoples' gameplay with the same effect.

The combat is super fun. It might get a little stale using the same weapon the whole game (I used the Thrust Stance all the way through) but it just makes the final boss more fun because [spoiler]he has your moveset BUT cooler and you will easily recognize these moves and lock in, due to already being familiar with their game[/spoiler]. Despite that, my favorite boss is actually a secret boss [spoiler]Erlang Shen[/spoiler], which was also the hardest boss here (22 attempts). He is super fun and has a great rhythm to the fight, which is really enough to sell me on a fight.

This game feels like it wants to be a Boss Rush with how many bosses there are, and it great! All bosses are well designed and fun to fight, except Yellow Loong, and Bishui Golden-Eyed Beast, those 2 are dookie and not fun. The Fire Mantle only makes the fight bearable, not fun. Honorable mention to Cyan Loong, but once you figure out his tell for his stupid twirl forward attack, he becomes easy.

If you plan to 100% this game, you are required to do a ng+, at least up to chapter 5 and fight the Bishui Golden-Eyed Beast again for some materials. LITERALLY I DON'T WANT TO FIGHT THAT THING AGAIN!!! I AM DONE WITH FIRE!!! 

-1 for the Bishui Golden-Eyed Beast.

The Best Game I've Ever Played!

Rating: 10/10 – An Absolute Masterpiece

I've been playing video games for years, but I can confidently say that Black Myth: Wukong is the best game I've ever played in my life.

Everything about this game is extraordinary. The breathtaking graphics, incredible environments, unforgettable boss fights, stunning soundtrack, and deep connection to Chinese mythology create an experience unlike anything I've played before.

What truly makes Wukong special is the attention to detail. Every location feels like a work of art, every battle feels meaningful, and every victory brings an incredible sense of achievement. The combat is challenging, rewarding, and incredibly satisfying. Even after hours of playing, I constantly find myself amazed by what this game has to offer.

But beyond the visuals and gameplay, there's something truly magical about its atmosphere, storytelling, and world. It's the kind of game that makes you want to explore every corner, discover every secret, and never let the adventure end.

Game Science has created something genuinely special. You can feel the passion, creativity, and dedication behind every part of this masterpiece.

I've played many incredible games throughout my life, but none has left such a lasting impression on me.

Black Myth: Wukong isn't just a great game. For me, it's the greatest gaming experience of my life.

I loved it at the beginning, but the more I progress the more boring it gets. You have magic abilities that do a huge amount of damage, but these have a long cooldown. They can also be interrupted, restaring the cooldown. For some bosses, doing melee attacks is almost useless so you basically run around waiting for the cooldowns to end. Some bosses have incredibly long combos that kill you off if you do not evade most of the attacks, and the drawn-out feeling of the boss fights makes learning them a chore.
You also frequently fight the camera, not only because sometimes you simply don't see anything if you stand near a wall or a tree, but also because it is very difficult to actually estimate the range of your charged melee attacks, so you charge up an attack only to have it end an inch in front of the boss. Bosses sometimes have a weakness or you can equip some item to make the fight a bit easier, but in many cases this is very obscure. Due to all this, beating a difficult boss did never feel like "yeah I earned this" but more often like "o.k., I was lucky  this time."

[h1][b]Black Myth: Wukong[/b][/h1]
[h3][b]My Journey to the West — 130+ Hours Later[/b][/h3]

I had not anticipated that the game would take more than 130 hours. And yet, I find myself approaching the conclusion of my personal "Journey to the West." I took a methodical approach, exploring at my own pace and occasionally optimising my equipment more than was necessary. I was pleasantly surprised by the extensive range of content available. Each chapter unveils new features and storylines, consistently maintaining my interest. I was rarely bored, and best of all, I was so immersed in the activity that I did not notice the time passing. Indeed, I am still playing to increase the difficulty with highly optimised gear.

[h3][b]Gameplay, Combat & Progression[/b][/h3]

In terms of gameplay, I found the difficulty level to be fairly balanced for a first playthrough. However, the difficulty level of some bosses was notably higher than others. I particularly appreciated the variety of skills and upgrades, which allowed for customisation of combat styles.

Depending on the boss, certain stances proved more effective than others to vary their approach rather than sticking to a single strategy. The game offers a wide range of weapons that prioritise power or critical hits, as well as skills that can be developed. In addition, there are armour sets that combine to offer additional bonuses, allowing plenty of room to experiment and fine-tune your setup.

The healing system is well-designed, with various flasks to unlock and drinks to combine for bonus effects. The bestiary is also impressive, featuring creatures and bosses with meticulous designs. 

The weapons and armour are impressive, and each discovery stimulates the desire to explore new possibilities. I would also like to express my appreciation of the ability to reset my skills at will, thus allowing me to experiment with different combat styles. Furthermore, I would have appreciated greater flexibility in the use of armour upgrade resources. In my personal experience, I have sometimes held back on certain items due to concerns about wasting them on equipment that I was planning to replace. This has sometimes resulted in missing out on potentially beneficial upgrades.

[h3][b]Visuals, Art Direction & Sound[/b][/h3]

Visually, I was extremely impressed. The settings in the various chapters are stunning, but it is the animation, the creatures' movements, and the visual effects that truly set this production apart. The art direction is a complete success. Even the animated sequences are charming and well-executed. The music skilfully transitions from a supporting role to a more prominent one during the most intense scenes. The key benefit of this approach is that it does not rely on visual cues or secondary characters to guide the user.

However, it should be noted that there are some aspects that could be improved. The most significant issue I have encountered is the presence of invisible walls, which can be frustrating when attempting to navigate detailed environments.

[h3][b]Story & Lore — A Journey Worth Knowing[/b][/h3]

In terms of the storyline, Black Myth: Wukong is set in a highly detailed universe, although the narrative world is not always clearly explained. The game draws inspiration from the famous Chinese novel Journey to the West, which recounts the journey of the monk Xuanzang to India, accompanied by the iconic Monkey King, Sun Wukong. This character is renowned for his cunning, his power, and his ability to shapeshift, making him an iconic figure in Chinese mythology. In addition, he was the source of inspiration for the character [b]Son Goku[/b] in the well-known manga [b]Dragon Ball.[/b]

I found the references to Chinese mythology to be of great interest. However, it should be noted that without prior knowledge of the subject, certain events may appear confusing and difficult to understand. At times, I would have preferred the storytelling to be more immersive, so as to better grasp the story's stakes. The animated sequences are of a high standard and significantly enhance the overall appeal of the adventure.

[h2][b]Conclusion — Worth the Wait[/b][/h2]

After such a long anticipation for this game, it was only natural to have some reservations, as is often the case when expectations are set too high. However, I was incorrect. Black Myth: Wukong met my expectations and even exceeded them thanks to the richness of its content. Despite a few minor issues, these are outweighed by the significant enjoyment derived from extensive gameplay.

I therefore have no hesitation in recommending it. The memorable combat, the exceptional bestiary, the sublime art direction, and an adventure that lasted much longer than expected all contributed to making this game a worthwhile purchase. Following 130 hours of gameplay, my sole objective is to reconnect with my team members and commence the adventure once more. Finally, it appears that the Monkey King has gained a valuable life lesson: material wealth is not necessarily a prerequisite for happiness. In contrast, the key elements of happiness are a capable team and the ability to overcome challenges. If you are having difficulty following the narrative, there is no cause for concern. Simply read Journey to the West, or acknowledge that the intricacies of Son Goku's tale exceeded initial expectations.
